content_list.content_text: Village of the Damned (1960) imagines a scenario in which society is subverted from within by a force that infiltrates children's minds; Night of the Eagle (1962) mixes witchcraft with questions of belief and superstition; Vargtimmen (Hour of the Wolf, 1968), by Bergman (1918-2007), a film about a relationship with elements of horror, addresses the role of art and the artist.

information.contentText: To make the scenes of satanic rituals and chants as realistic as possible, director Roman Polanski enlisted the help of Anton LaVey, founder of the Church of Satan and author of "The Satanic Bible," who served as a consultant on these scenes.

content_list.content_text: Even the master of exploitation film, Roger Corman (b. 1926), found time amid the decadence and theatricality of The Masque of the Red Death (1964) to discuss the nature of religious faith. The most interesting discussions took place, perhaps, in the films that focused on contemporary society.

There are clear anti-bourgeois diatribes in the grotesque revels of the rich depicted in Corman's Poe cycle, in Roger Vadim's (1928-2000) segment of Histoires extraordinaires (Spirits of the Dead, 1968) and, finally, in the coven of witches on Manhattan's Upper West Side in Rosemary's Baby (1968).

information.contentTitle: Scene from Night of the Living Dead
information.contentText: George Romero produced the film on a budget of US$114,000, and after a decade of theatrical re-releases it had grossed around $12 million domestically and US$30 million internationally. On its release in 1968, Night of the Living Dead was heavily criticized for its explicit content. In 1999, the United States Library of Congress added it to its National Film Registry as a film deemed "historically, culturally, or aesthetically significant."

content_list.description: A quick look at George Romero's debut and the copyright issues that shaped the zombie genre.

content_list.title: Satanic Cinema
content_list.description: The devil made an early debut in cinema. In Le Manoir du diable (1896), director Georges Méliès (1861-1938) plays Mephistopheles. The best version of the Faust legend is still Faust (1926), by F. W. Murnau (1888-1931), but pacts with the devil have appeared in other films such as The Devil and Daniel Webster (1941) and The Devil's Advocate (1997). Many dramas, such as Wall Street (1987) and The Devil Wears Prada (2006), boil down to a new guise for the Faust story, adorned with the specific concerns of their era. Devil worship crept into cinema mainly as a threat, as in The Seventh Victim (1943), whose New York coven prefigures Ira Levin's, as well as in Hammer's boisterous The Devil Rides Out (1967). One of cinema's best devils was Robert De Niro (b. 1943) in Angel Heart (1987).

content_list.content_text: It can be read as a 1960s condemnation of the greedy, in the postwar spirit of equality and civil liberties; Witchfinder General (1968) is a forceful reminder of historical atrocities and also a brutal metaphor for Senator McCarthy's anticommunist witch hunt of the 1950s. Low-budget horror cinema came to the fore in films such as Night of the Living Dead (1968), by George A. Romero (b. 1940), which questioned whether the world is good and morally just.

With intense close-ups, tilted cameras and well-developed characters, this new wave marked the arrival of the independent director and alerted audiences to new concerns. The zombies (revived by the effects of radiation) can be seen as references to racism and war. Unlike many other horror films, the danger extends to the whole country, perhaps even the whole world.

information.contentText: When originally made, the film was seen as a departure from Hitchcock's previous work, having been shot on a low budget, with a television crew and in black and white. Psycho initially received mixed reviews but, thanks to its excellent box office, the film was reappraised, which led to critical acclaim and four Oscar nominations, including Best Supporting Actress for Leigh and Best Director for Hitchcock.

content_list.content_text: Beyond the supernatural evil of The Haunting (1963) and the alien invaders of The Day of the Triffids (1962), horror cinema also took on a human face. The danger could be anyone and the terror was real, as in Peeping Tom (1960) and Psycho (1960). With The Birds (1963), Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) once again subverted what audiences expect of a heroine.

quote.quote: Some of my most praised films – Rosemary's Baby, Repulsion, The Tenant – dealt largely with questions of living together... I wouldn't have chosen them.
quote.author: Roman Polanski

content_list.content_text: The classic female lead in horror films is the virginal blonde dressed in white who acts as a moral compass: the kindhearted Mina survives Dracula, whereas having sex can have sinister consequences, as happened to Mia Farrow in Rosemary's Baby. Unlike the vast majority of female leads in horror films, Tippi Hedren's (b. 1930) Melanie in The Birds is no wilting violet, but a confident woman who pursues a man all the way to his front door. With that, female characters came to have a far greater range than their mere terrified stares.

information.contentText: The sinister children of Village of the Damned have blond hair, striking eyes, and telepathic powers they use to protect themselves.

content_list.content_text: The horror film was popular not only in the United States but also in Europe and Asia. The supernatural Onibaba (1964) and Kwaidan (1964) mark the invasion of Japanese horror 30 years before Ringu (Ring, 1998). Giallo films made the careers of many European directors, such as Dario Argento (b. 1940).

French horror films had little impact despite the chilling Les Yeux sans visage (Eyes Without a Face, 1960), but French ancestry can be attributed to films influenced by the Grand Guignol movement, such as the stylized horror (more specifically Grande Dame Guignol) of What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962) and the lavish output of Hammer. With a core trio formed by director Terence Fisher (1904-1980) and actors Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing, Hammer became Britain's leading studio, regularly producing films such as Dracula: Prince of Darkness (1966) and Frankenstein Must Be Destroyed (1969) and, at its peak, The Devil Rides Out (1968), with a screenplay by Richard Matheson (1926-2013).

information.contentText: Montage editing and slow pacing are used throughout the film to build suspense and draw a stronger emotional response from the audience during the attack scenes: "The pattern of The Birds was deliberately to go slow." This is exemplified in the scene in which the birds gradually gather outside the school while Melanie, unaware, sits and waits on the bench. The camera cuts between her and the growing number of birds crowding onto the jungle gym behind her until they finally attack.

content_list.content_text: In Western cinemas, the 1960s were the era when horror films were respected as art. However, it was also the decade in which the genre began to lose focus. The studios realized they could churn out endless sequels and crude imitations. The horror film became a cheap commodity and the drive-in became a home for exploitation fare. Nevertheless, this type of film gave 1960s filmmaking a reach and scope that flourished until the arrival and saturation of the B-movie market of the Jason genre.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Simon Ward, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

content_list.content_text: It is practically impossible to imagine a world without zombie films. The subgenre has been so heavily explored - even outside horror - that many people see such stories as oversaturated. On October 1, 1968, that wasn't quite the case, and if it weren't for a bureaucratic error involving Night of the Living Dead, it's quite possible that all of today's popularity would never have existed.
content_list.content_title: How a bureaucratic error popularized zombie films

information.contentText: Props and special effects were simple and limited by the budget. The blood, for example, was Bosco Chocolate Syrup poured over the cast members' bodies. The flesh being eaten was roast ham. The costumes consisted of secondhand clothes, and mortician's wax served as makeup for the zombies. Marilyn Eastman oversaw special effects, costumes and makeup. Filming took place between June and December 1967 under the working title Night of Anubis, and later Night of the Flesh Eaters. The low budget led Romero to shoot on 35 mm black-and-white film. In the end, the finished film benefited from this decision; film historian Joseph Maddrey describes the black-and-white photography as "guerrilla-style," resembling "the unflinching authority of wartime newsreels." Maddrey adds that it "seems as much a documentary on the loss of social stability as an exploitation film."
information.source: Night of the Living Dead LLC, via Image Ten

content_list.content_text: George Romero's work deserves full credit on its own: the film is a landmark of low-budget cinema that not only establishes the threat of the undead horde but also delivers tension and action combined with a solid layer of social commentary, featuring a Black hero who defies the stereotypes of the time - and a treacherous ending with timeless impact. The feature also doesn't hold back on violence, something that caught 1960s audiences off guard, especially considering there was no age-rating system to control who watched it in theaters: "The movie had stopped being delightfully scary about halfway through, and had become unexpectedly terrifying," wrote Roger Ebert, critic for the Chicago Sun-Times. "There was a little girl across the aisle from me, maybe nine years old, who was sitting very still in her seat and crying."

But what elevated Night of the Living Dead from a great film into a true cultural phenomenon has to do not only with its content but also with its distribution. As it happens, the film was originally called Night of the Flesh Eaters (or A Noite dos Devoradores de Carne, in a loose Portuguese translation) but, since the name was very similar to that of The Flesh Eaters (1964), the distributor Walter Reade Organization asked for the title to be changed to Night of the Living Dead. The sudden change came with a slip: to secure copyright on an audiovisual work at the time, the copyright symbol (©) had to appear in the film's opening. When the title was changed, the production forgot to include the notice of intellectual property. Just a tiny mistake, right?

In fact, the absence of the symbol meant that Night of the Living Dead was released straight into the public domain; in other words, anyone could simply get a copy and screen it publicly as many times as they wanted, even charging admission. While this may have hurt the original distributor's pocket, since it wasn't collecting the box-office takings, the accident allowed the film to be widely shown at smaller events, small theaters, drive-ins and every kind of venue that wanted to screen the much-talked-about indie horror.

information.contentText: The film's famous opening. Notice how at 00:41 the copyright (©) is missing.
information.source: YouTube: Decay is headed your way! channel

content_list.content_text: Moreover, the public domain also allows different creators to contribute to the characters and concepts of the work in question. Basically any filmmaker could now use Romero's zombies in their projects - and that is exactly what happened, with a veritable infestation of films about the walking dead. The best example of this perhaps comes from Italy, a prolific low-budget film industry, which launched major filmmakers through imitations and reinterpretations of the American film, such as Zombi 2 (Zombie Flesh Eaters, 1979), an unofficial sequel to Night of the Living Dead by horror master Lucio Fulci (1927-1996).

The film remains in the public domain to this day and is available in full on the Internet Archive and even on YouTube. Nor was the work hurt much by what happened, grossing US$30 million on a tiny budget of US$110,000.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "Noite dos Mortos-Vivos | Como um erro burocrático popularizou os filmes de zumbi" (Night of the Living Dead | How a bureaucratic error popularized zombie films), by Arthur Eloi on Omelete.com

movies.title: Psycho
movies.overview: When larcenous real estate clerk Marion Crane goes on the lam with a wad of cash and hopes of starting a new life, she ends up at the notorious Bates Motel, where manager Norman Bates cares for his housebound mother.

movies.title: The Haunting
movies.overview: Dr. Markway, doing research to prove the existence of ghosts, investigates Hill House, a large, eerie mansion with a lurid history of violent death and insanity.

movies.title: Rosemary's Baby
movies.overview: A young couple moves into an infamous New York apartment building to start a family. Things become frightening as Rosemary begins to suspect her unborn baby isn’t safe around their strange neighbors.

movies.title: Night of the Living Dead
movies.overview: A group of people try to survive an attack of bloodthirsty zombies while trapped in a rural Pennsylvania farmhouse.

movies.title: Night of the Eagle
movies.overview: A skeptical college professor discovers that his wife has been practicing magic for years. Like the learned, rational fellow he is, he forces her to destroy all her magical charms and protective devices, and stop that foolishness. He isn't put off by her insistence that his professional rivals are working magic against him, and her protections are necessary to his career and life.

movies.title: Spirits of the Dead
movies.overview: Three directors each adapt a Poe short story to the screen: "Toby Dammit" features a disheveled drugged and drunk English movie star who nods acceptance in the Italian press and his producers fawn over him. "Metzengerstein" features a Mediveal countess who has a love-hate relationship with a black stallion - who it turns out is really her dead lover. "William Wilson" tells the story of a sadistic Austrian student with an exact double whom he later kills.

movies.title: Witchfinder General
movies.overview: England, 1645. The cruel civil war between Royalists and Parliamentarians that is ravaging the country causes an era of chaos and legal arbitrariness that allows unscrupulous men to profit by exploiting the absurd superstitions of the peasants; like Matthew Hopkins, a monster disguised as a man who wanders from town to town offering his services as a witch hunter.

movies.title: The Day of the Triffids
movies.overview: A shower of meteorites produces a rare night time spectacle that blinds anyone that looks at it. As it was such a beautiful sight, most people were watching, and as a consequence, 99% of the World's population go completely blind. In the original novel, this chaos results in the escape of Triffids: farmed plants harvested for their oils, which are capable of moving themselves around and are carnivorous. In this film version, however, the Triffids are not indigenous plants. Instead they are space aliens whose spores have arrived in this and an earlier meteor shower.  Derided by the original novel's author, John Wyndham, for straying so far away from the source material.

movies.title: The Birds
movies.overview: Chic socialite Melanie Daniels enjoys a passing flirtation with an eligible attorney in a San Francisco pet shop and, on an impulse, follows him to his hometown bearing a gift of lovebirds. But upon her arrival, the bird population runs amok. Suddenly, the townsfolk face a massive avian onslaught, with the feathered fiends inexplicably attacking people all over Bodega Bay.

movies.title: Eyes Without a Face
movies.overview: Dr. Génessier is riddled with guilt after an accident that he caused disfigures the face of his daughter, the once beautiful Christiane, who outsiders believe is dead. Dr. Génessier, along with accomplice and laboratory assistant Louise, kidnaps young women and brings them to the Génessier mansion. After rendering his victims unconscious, Dr. Génessier removes their faces and attempts to graft them on to Christiane's.

movies.original_title: What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?
movies.title: What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?
movies.overview: Two aging film actresses live as virtual recluses in an old Hollywood mansion. Jane Hudson, a successful child star, cares for her crippled sister Blanche, whose career in later years eclipsed that of Jane. Now the two live together, their relationship affected by simmering subconscious thoughts of mutual envy, hate and revenge.

movies.title: Dracula: Prince of Darkness
movies.overview: Whilst vacationing in the Carpathian Mountain, two couples stumble across the remains of Count Dracula's castle. The Count's trusted servant kills one of the men, suspending the body over the Count's ashes so that the blood drips from the corpse and saturates the blackened remains. The ritual is completed, the Count revived and his attentions focus on the dead man's wife who is to become his partner; devoted to an existence of depravity and evil.
